messages:
hannah_support: Customer reported intermittent 429s during short traffic spikes. They said it only happens for ~10-30s at a time and then everything recovers. They included a snippet of headers and a short curl they used.

hannah_support: Key bits from customer: requests spike from 20rps to 400rps for ~15s; they see: 

  HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
  Retry-After: 3
  X-RateLimit-Limit: 300
  X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
  X-RateLimit-Reset: 1670000123

They asked: do we have burst credits? can short bursts bypass quota? why Retry-After is small but still hits hard?

liz_oncall: @hannah_support assigning to runtime / rate-limits. tagging @raj_eng_runtime for config details.

raj_eng_runtime: quick notes: our rate limiter is a token-bucket per-customer per-route with a short-term burst bucket and a steady refill rate. burst tokens are meant for short spikes but are finite and don't persist across long windows. sounds like their spike exhausted burst tokens then started hitting steady quota limits.

raj_eng_runtime: couple of things to check from their end:
- whether requests are hitting multiple routes (per-route quotas) or a single endpoint
- if they're using many small concurrent clients (each client can create concurrent connections that amplify instantaneous rps)
- whether they obey Retry-After / implement jittered backoff

hannah_support: pasted their repro command: 

  for i in {1..400}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H 'Authorization: Bearer <KEY>' \"https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate\" & done

They basically fired 400 parallel requests.

mike_product: FYI this pattern (many parallel short requests) tends to blow through burst buckets. Product wise we should document guidance about smoothing and client-side token bucket.

raj_eng_runtime: suggested mitigation for customer:
1) Add a client-side smoothing layer (small queue + rate limiter). e.g. token-bucket at 50-100rps if their long-term average supports it.
2) Use exponential backoff honoring Retry-After with random jitter.
3) If using Reserved/Dedicated capacity, request a temporary increase to burst_tokens (we can raise max_burst_tokens per-customer for a short period).

liz_oncall: @raj_eng_runtime can you confirm what we bill against when burst tokens are consumed? customer worried bursts will blow up their invoice.

billing-bot: burst consumption is billed as normal usage; reserved capacity customers consume their committed throughput first, then bursts count towards overage or usage depending on their contract. Non-reserved (hosted) customers pay per-token usage as usual.

raj_eng_runtime: technical: our default bucket settings are: steady_rate = 10rps (per-route default), max_burst_tokens = 300 tokens, burst_window ~ 30s. If they go from 20rps -> 400rps, 300 tokens will be used in ~1s, then they hit steady limit and get 429s. Retry-After tends to be small because reset is soon but repeated bursts keep exhausting buckets.

hannah_support: customer asked whether we can "smooth" traffic server-side to absorb spikes gracefully rather than immediately 429.

raj_eng_runtime: server-side smoothing options:
- increase max_burst_tokens for the customer (temporary uplift). good for planned traffic bursts.
- implement short-term leaky bucket queuing with a small, bounded request queue (adds a couple hundred ms latency but avoids 429s for very short spikes). this is a runtime change and needs ops/infra approval; risk: queues can increase memory/use under sustained spikes.
- per-route fractional throttling: allow X% of requests above quota to be probabilistically accepted (useful to avoid synchronized retries causing thundering herd).

mike_product: tradeoffs: smoothing benefits UX but increases p95 latency and could hide bad client behavior. recommend doc + client-side best practices + temporary server-side boost for high-value customers.

hannah_support: proposed reply to customer: 
1) explain burst token mechanics concisely, show their logs mapping to tokens used.
2) recommend immediate client-side mitigation (smoothing + backoff) with example code.
3) offer a temporary bump to their burst_tokens for an upcoming campaign; note billing implications.
4) if they want permanent changes, open a dedicated ops ticket to evaluate queuing or probabilistic acceptance.

raj_eng_runtime: example smoothing snippet to send them: 

```python
# very small client-side leaky bucket
import time, threading
from queue import Queue
q = Queue()
RATE = 100  # target rps

def worker():
    while True:
        req = q.get()
        make_request(req)
        time.sleep(1.0 / RATE)

threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
# push into q at burst arrival; worker paces to RATE
```

raj_eng_runtime: also sample header-based guidance: check X-RateLimit-Remaining to decide whether to slow down. if Remaining <= 5, start exponential backoff immediately.

liz_oncall: fine. @hannah_support go ahead and offer the temporary increase and include the snippet. put follow-up ticket to eng-runtime to consider per-route leaky queue as an opt-in config.

hannah_support: will do. final note for the thread: ask customer to provide one spike trace (logs + request ids) so we can audit whether requests were batched across regions or routes.

ops-bot: Created ticket INF-4921 for eng-runtime to evaluate queueing option.

hannah_support: thanks everyone. I'll reply to the customer with the plan and mark the thread as escalated to INF-4921 if they accept the temporary boost. :thumbsup:
